summary: Defines an NNTP extension that lets a connection between client and server be compressed, saving bandwidth for Usenet news transfer.

eli5.summary: News messages are packed into a smaller bag before being sent, then unpacked, so less is carried.

questions: how to compress an nntp connection
why no authentication after compress in nntp
subtitle: A single NNTP command that compresses everything the client and server say to each other afterwards.

tldr.problem: News traffic uses a lot of bandwidth, and the existing ways of compressing it were unstandardized commands that only compressed server responses, or TLS-level compression, which best current practice says to disable.
tldr.mechanism: The COMPRESS extension adds a COMPRESS command. After the server answers 206, a compression layer using DEFLATE covers all commands and responses in both directions.
tldr.outcome: Compression can be switched on at a chosen moment, such as after authentication. It must be applied before encryption, and authentication is forbidden once it is active.

today: RFC 8054 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the specification of the NNTP COMPRESS extension.

sections.title: Why NNTP Needs a Compression Layer
sections.content:
The goal of COMPRESS is to reduce the bandwidth usage of NNTP, the Network News Transfer Protocol defined in RFC 3977. It acts as a compression layer, similar to the security layer negotiated by STARTTLS (RFC 4642), so it helps every NNTP command sent or received after it is used.

The RFC says this answers a long-standing need. Until then, only unstandardized commands such as XZVER, XZHDR, XFEATURE COMPRESS or MODE COMPRESS existed, and they compress only the responses sent by the news server. COMPRESS covers data sent by both client and server, and it removes the need to implement compression separately in each command. Once COMPRESS is supported, using other commands to enable compression is discouraged.

To keep interoperability simple, the document specifies only one algorithm. DEFLATE, defined in RFC 1951, MUST be implemented. Where this document conflicts with RFC 3977, RFC 3977 takes precedence.
sections.eli5: Instead of every kind of news message having its own way to shrink, there is one switch that shrinks everything said in both directions.

sections.title: Advertising the Extension
sections.content:
A server that supports the command lists the COMPRESS capability label in its answer to the CAPABILITIES command. The label carries a whitespace-separated list of algorithms. DEFLATE is the only one this document defines, and it MUST be supported and listed. Clients MUST ignore algorithms they do not recognize, so later extensions can add more.

The server MUST NOT advertise the capability once a compression layer is active. Because compression can weaken encryption, a client MUST NOT rely on capabilities cached from an earlier session.

The capability may be advertised both before and after MODE READER, with the same meaning.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a menu saying which kinds of squashing it knows. The client ignores any item on the menu it has never heard of.

sections.title: The COMPRESS Command
sections.content:
The syntax is COMPRESS algorithm, and the command MUST NOT be pipelined. The client MUST NOT send anything else until it sees the result. The possible responses are 206 (compression active), 403 (unable to activate compression) and 502 (command unavailable, for example because a compression layer is already active). A syntactically incorrect algorithm name gets 501, and an unsupported one gets 503.

On 206, the compression layer takes effect for both sides immediately after the CRLF of the success reply. Both ends MUST know whether a layer is active, whether from COMPRESS or from TLS-level compression. A client MUST NOT try to compress or negotiate STARTTLS when a layer is active, and the server answers 502 if it sees such a command.

After COMPRESS, the client MUST NOT issue MODE READER, and the server MUST NOT advertise the MODE-READER capability. If either side receives invalid or corrupted compressed data, it closes the connection immediately and the other end does the same.
sections.eli5: The client says 'let us squash from now on', waits for a yes, and from the very next word everything is squashed. If a squashed message arrives broken, both sides hang up.

sections.title: Layering with TLS and SASL
sections.content:
When COMPRESS is combined with TLS (RFC 5246) or SASL (RFC 4422) security layers, the processing order MUST be first COMPRESS, then SASL, and finally TLS. Data is compressed before it is signed or encrypted, and the order is reversed on receipt.

The RFC lists advantages over TLS-level compression (RFC 3749), which best current practice says to disable (RFC 7525). COMPRESS is easy to implement for both servers and clients. It benefits from intimate knowledge of the NNTP state machine, which allows dynamic tuning of the algorithm. It can also be activated after authentication has completed.
sections.eli5: First you squash the letter, then you lock it in a box. You cannot squash a locked box, so the order matters.

sections.title: Compression Efficiency and DEFLATE Tips
sections.content:
The informative section 3 explains that NNTP is an unusual case. Using its least CPU-intensive setting, zlib compresses typical multi-line responses (for example to LIST, LISTGROUP, NEWGROUPS and NEWNEWS) to 25-40% of their original size. Article headers and text bodies compress well too, and simple one-line responses generally save few bytes.

Non-text attachments are the hard case. Base64 or UUencode data usually compresses to only about 75% of its encoded size, and yEnc data is much more likely to be incompressible. The RFC therefore suggests that a server change the compression level around such blocks, for example setting level 0 at the start of an incompressible block and keeping it at 1-5 the rest of the time.

For zlib, section 4 says the windowBits value MUST be in the range -8 to -15 for deflateInit2() and SHOULD be -15 for inflateInit2(). The receiver MUST adjust automatically to the sender's parameters, and all submitted data MUST be flushed so the receiver can fully decompress it.
sections.eli5: Lists of words squash into a tiny bundle, but things that are already tightly packed, like a photo sent as text, do not squash much. So the server stops trying for those.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compression combined with encryption can reveal information. An adversary who sees the length of the compressed data may be able to derive facts about the plain data. The CRIME and BREACH attacks are examples (RFC 7457).

To protect credentials, authentication MUST NOT be attempted after a successful COMPRESS. After COMPRESS, the server lists AUTHINFO with no arguments or not at all, and answers 502 to an AUTHINFO command. A client that wants STARTTLS, authentication and compression in one connection MUST use STARTTLS, then AUTHINFO, then COMPRESS, in that order. Implicit TLS on a dedicated port is also allowed.

For private newsgroups, implementations SHOULD NOT compress confidential data together with public data when a TLS or SASL layer is active. Clearing the DEFLATE dictionary each time a confidential article is sent is one way to avoid mixing articles. Implementations SHOULD NOT automatically enable compression with a security layer active unless the user explicitly enabled it.
sections.eli5: If someone can see how big your squashed package is, they can sometimes guess what is inside. So log in first, and only then start squashing.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA maintains a new "NNTP Compression Algorithms" registry. Names are 1 to 20 characters of uppercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, and registration is First Come First Served as defined in BCP 26. Unregistered private algorithms are allowed but SHOULD NOT be used because interoperability is hard. Entries are never deleted, but can be marked OBSOLETE.

The registry holds one entry, DEFLATE, with intended usage COMMON, mandatory to implement, with the IESG as change controller. The COMPRESS label is also added to the "NNTP Capability Labels" registry, and the document defines the new response code 206.
sections.eli5: There is an official phone book of squashing methods, so two programs can be sure they mean the same one by a given name.

items.desc: The algorithm name is syntactically incorrect.

items.desc: A compression layer is already active.

items.desc: The requested algorithm is invalid, for example unsupported.
